# Yongwang: the stories first, then the spelling

Before the spelling, the story. **Yongwang** earns its restoration the old way — through what was actually told.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Python and the Wish-Jewel.** The Samguk Yusa, “Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms” (13th century), tells of a poor but kind-hearted man who gave shelter to a strange traveller caught by night and rain.  The stranger revealed himself as an imugi — a python that had waited a thousand years for the yeouiju, the wish-granting jewel that alone can raise a serpent to dragonhood.  Entrusting the jewel to his host, the imugi attempted the ascent to heaven; when it slipped, the man caught it and set it upon the serpent’s head, and the imugi became a true dragon and rose into the sky.

**The King Who Became a Dragon.** The Samguk Sagi and Samguk Yusa record that King Munmu of Silla (r.  661–681), dying, commanded that his body be cremated and the ashes cast into the East Sea.  “I will become a dragon,” he said, “and protect this kingdom from the pirates of the east.

**The Yongwang-gut of the Fishing Villages.** In the fishing villages of Korea’s south coast — Chaeseon in Tongyeong, Suyeong in Busan — shamans performed the Yongwang-gut, the rite of the Dragon King, to open the fishing season and beg calm seas.  The folklorist Im Seok-jae recorded these rites in the twentieth century, when they were already old: the shaman invokes the dragon kings of the four seas in turn, receives their possessing presence, and sends a paper dragon-boat laden with rice, fruit, cloth, and coins out onto the water, the offering itself sailing to the palace beneath the waves.  If the season proves good, the debt is remembered; if storms come, the rite is repeated with greater care.

## The Name Travels

Yongwang is part of a broader East Asian dragon-king tradition, with close parallels in Chinese, Japanese, and Vietnamese religion; the Sino-Korean name itself, 龍王, is borrowed directly.  In Korea the figure was absorbed into both Buddhism and shamanism: he appears as a deva-like guardian and rain-maker in Buddhist temples, and as a sovereign spirit who must be formally petitioned in gut rituals.
